implementation_notes: In Akka the return address is the sender reference attached to a message: classic actors answer with sender() ! reply, and ask (?) installs a temporary actor as the sender so the caller receives a Future, requiring an implicit Timeout and failing with AskTimeoutException when nothing answers. Typed actors make the address explicit with context.ask or by carrying an ActorRef[Response] in the message. Use ask when the caller needs the result, explicit ActorRef passing when replies must be routed to another component, and remember the ActorRef is the address — it must be remotely addressable to survive a node boundary.
idiom_name: Akka ask (?) with the implicit sender() as return address
pitfalls: sender() is only valid while handling a message — capturing it in a Future callback or a child actor's closure sends the reply to dead letters.
ask allocates a temporary actor per call and needs a timeout; high-frequency unary asks are better served by an ActorRef[Response] in the message or askWithReplyTo.
An ActorRef only works as a return address if it is remotely addressable (Cluster/Remoting with a serializer), otherwise replies cannot cross nodes.
